pos: n. (morbid drowsiness; dullness of spirit; the sleep that overtakes a soul with work to do)
etymology: Greek lethargia, from lethe, forgetfulness, and argos, idle. The forgetting and the idleness are joined in the word: a man grows dull because he has stopped remembering what is at stake.
biblical_def: Lethargy is spiritual drowsiness. Paul makes the hour the argument: “knowing the time, that now it is high time to awake out of sleep: for now is our salvation nearer than when we believed” (Rom 13:11). Proverbs presses the sluggard: “How long wilt thou sleep, O sluggard? when wilt thou arise out of thy sleep? Yet a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep” (Pro 6:9–10). In the parable, the wise virgins are no more awake than the foolish: “while the bridegroom tarried, they all slumbered and slept” (Mat 25:5). The call is a summons from the dead: “Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light” (Eph 5:14). And the Lord asks it personally: “Simon, sleepest thou? couldest not thou watch one hour?” (Mar 14:37).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines lethargy as morbid drowsiness; preternatural sleepiness; and dullness, inaction, inattention.
webster_full: LETHARGY, n. Preternatural sleepiness; morbid drowsiness; continued or profound sleep, from which a person can scarcely be awaked.
2. Dullness; inaction; inattention.
LETHARGIC, a. Preternaturally inclined to sleep; drowsy; dull; heavy.
scriptures: And that, knowing the time, that now it is high time to awake out of sleep: for now is our salvation nearer than when we believed.
Pro 6:9
How long wilt thou sleep, O sluggard? when wilt thou arise out of thy sleep?
Mat 25:5
While the bridegroom tarried, they all slumbered and slept.
Eph 5:14
Wherefore he saith, Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light.
And he cometh, and findeth them sleeping, and saith unto Peter, Simon, sleepest thou? couldest not thou watch one hour?
corruption_summary: Spiritual dullness is mistaken for peace, and the sluggard's own account of himself is always that a little more sleep is reasonable.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 6:10 is the sluggard's inner monologue reproduced exactly, and its power is in the diminutives: yet a little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands. Nothing in it is a decision to waste a life. Each instalment is small, defensible and temporary, and the ruin described in the next verse arrives as a traveller — steadily, on its own schedule, without being invited. That is the mechanism of spiritual decline in most Christians. Almost no one resolves to drift; they postpone, in small units, for reasons that are individually sound.

Matthew 25:5 removes the comfort of comparison, and it is the detail preachers most often skip: they all slumbered and slept. Both parties. The wise virgins were no more alert than the foolish, and the difference between them was not vigilance in the night but oil bought beforehand. The parable therefore refuses to make watchfulness a matter of maintaining a constant emotional intensity, which no one can do; it makes it a matter of preparation made while there was time.

Mark 14:37 is the tenderest and most searching of these texts. Simon, sleepest thou? couldest not thou watch one hour? — and the Lord adds, the spirit truly is ready, but the flesh is weak, which is a diagnosis rather than an excuse and comes from the One who knows exactly how weak. Ephesians 5:14 supplies the only remedy that ever works: awake, arise, and Christ shall give thee light. A sleeper cannot rouse himself by resolution; the command is issued with the promise attached, and the light comes from outside the man.
roots_summary: Greek hupnos (G5258), sleep; gregoreo (G1127), to watch, stay awake; nustazo (G3573), to nod, slumber; Hebrew atsel (H6102), sluggard.
roots_lines: Greek ex hupnou egerthenai (G5258) — to awake out of sleep; Romans 13:11.
Greek gregoreo (G1127) — to watch; Mark 14:34–38, Matthew 25:13, 1 Thessalonians 5:6, 1 Peter 5:8.
Hebrew atsel (H6102) — sluggard; Proverbs 6:6–9, 13:4, 20:4, 26:14–16.
usage: “A little sleep, a little slumber” — each instalment defensible.
“They all slumbered and slept” — both parties, and the oil was the difference.
“Awake… and Christ shall give thee light” — the promise is attached.

pos: n. (lightness of temper or conduct; want of due seriousness in weighty things)
etymology: Latin levitas, lightness, from levis, light — the opposite of gravitas, weight. Jeremiah's own word for false prophets is lightness (Jer 23:32).
biblical_def: Levity is lightness where weight is owed. Paul forbids one variety: “neither filthiness, nor foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not convenient: but rather giving of thanks” (Eph 5:4). The Preacher weighs the fool's mirth: “as the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of the fool” (Ecc 7:6). Proverbs exposes the man who wounds and then claims he was only playing: “So is the man that deceiveth his neighbour, and saith, Am not I in sport?” (Pro 26:19). Jeremiah charges the prophets with it: they “cause my people to err by their lies, and by their lightness” (Jer 23:32). Yet laughter itself is appointed: “a time to weep, and a time to laugh” (Ecc 3:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines levity as lightness; inconstancy; want of due consideration; unbecoming trifling; and vanity, want of seriousness.
webster_full: LEVITY, n. Lightness; the want of weight in a body, compared with another that is heavier.
2. Lightness of temper or conduct; inconstancy; changeableness; unsteadiness.
3. Want of due consideration; vanity; freak.
4. Trifling gaiety; want of seriousness; disposition to trifle.
scriptures: Eph 5:4
Neither filthiness, nor foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not convenient: but rather giving of thanks.
Ecc 7:6
For as the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of the fool: this also is vanity.
So is the man that deceiveth his neighbour, and saith, Am not I in sport?

Behold, I am against them that prophesy false dreams, saith the LORD, and do tell them, and cause my people to err by their lies, and by their lightness; yet I sent them not, nor commanded them: therefore they shall not profit this people at all, saith the LORD.
Ecc 3:4
A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance;
corruption_summary: Seriousness is confused with solemnity, and the Bible forbids the one kind of joking while appointing a time to laugh.
corruption_paragraphs: Ephesians 5:4 is not a prohibition of humour and reads badly if taken that way, since the same Paul uses irony, sarcasm and at least one joke about his opponents that no commentator likes to translate plainly. The word rendered jesting means well-turned speech, and its fault in context is set by the company it keeps: filthiness and foolish talking. What is forbidden is wit deployed to make the shameful amusing — the deftness that lets a room laugh at what it ought to be grieved by. The alternative Paul names is not gravity but giving of thanks, which is a cheerful thing.

Proverbs 26:19 catches the commonest use of levity in relationships, and it is not comic at all. A man deceives his neighbour and then says, Am not I in sport? — the joke as an escape hatch, allowing a thing to be said and then disowned. The preceding verse compares him to a madman casting firebrands, arrows and death, which is a startling proportion to assign to teasing. The reason is that this manoeuvre makes correction impossible: the offence was real and the offender has pre-emptively defined it as unreal, so the wounded party is left with nothing to answer.

The opposite error is the confusion of seriousness with heaviness, and it produces a religion that is not attractive because it is not true. Ecclesiastes 3:4 appoints a time to laugh; the Lord's teaching is full of comic exaggeration — a camel through a needle's eye, a man with a plank in his eye offering eye surgery — and the joy commanded in Philippians is not a subdued thing. Ecclesiastes 7:6 is precise about what it condemns: the crackling of thorns under a pot, a great noise and a brief flare that boils nothing. The fault of the fool's laughter is not that it is laughter but that there is nothing underneath it.
roots_summary: Greek eutrapelia (G2160), jesting, ready wit; morologia (G3473), foolish talking; Hebrew pachaz (H6350), lightness, wantonness; sechoq (H7814), laughter.
roots_lines: Greek eutrapelia (G2160) — jesting, coarse wit; Ephesians 5:4 only.
Greek morologia (G3473) — foolish talking; Ephesians 5:4 only.
Hebrew pachazuth (H6350) — lightness, recklessness; Jeremiah 23:32, Zephaniah 3:4.
usage: “Nor jesting, which are not convenient” — and the alternative is thanksgiving.
“Am not I in sport?” — the joke as an escape hatch.
“The crackling of thorns under a pot” — a great noise that boils nothing.

pos: adj. (anxiously careful; concerned to the point of disquiet)
etymology: Latin sollicitus, thoroughly stirred up, from sollus, whole, and ciere, to move. The AV's word for this state is careful, in its older sense of full of care.
biblical_def: To be solicitous is to be anxiously careful, which is what the AV means by careful. Paul forbids it and supplies the substitute: “Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God” (Php 4:6). The Lord forbids it three times in one passage: “Take no thought for your life, what ye shall eat, or what ye shall drink” (Mat 6:25), and “Take therefore no thought for the morrow… sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof” (Mat 6:34). He names it gently in a friend: “Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things: but one thing is needful” (Luk 10:41–42). And Peter gives the transfer: “Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you” (1Pe 5:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines solicitous as anxious; very desirous, as to obtain something; careful; concerned.
webster_full: SOLICITOUS, a. Anxious; very desirous, as to obtain something; careful; concerned.
The colonel was solicitous to make his men comfortable.
SOLICITUDE, n. Uneasiness of mind occasioned by the fear of evil or the desire of good; anxiety; carefulness.
scriptures: Php 4:6
Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God.
Mat 6:25

Therefore I say unto you, Take no thought for your life, what ye shall eat, or what ye shall drink; nor yet for your body, what ye shall put on. Is not the life more than meat, and the body than raiment?
Mat 6:34
Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.
And Jesus answered and said unto her, Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things:
Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you.
corruption_summary: Anxiety is treated as a temperament or a virtue, and Scripture treats it as a form of care aimed at the wrong address.
corruption_paragraphs: The commonest misreading is to hear these texts as a demand to stop feeling anxious, which is not a thing anyone can do on command, and to conclude that the anxious Christian is failing at something basic. But Philippians 4:6 does not stop at the prohibition; it names a replacement, and the sentence is built so that the negative is only half of it. Be careful for nothing — but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known. The care is not to be extinguished. It is to be moved, item by item, to a place where it can do something.

First Peter 5:7 gives the same movement in a single image with a reason attached: casting all your care upon him, for he careth for you. The two English words are different in Greek — the care cast is anxiety, the care He has is concern — and the logic is that a man may hand over his worry because Someone else is already carrying the interest. That is why the verse comes immediately after a command to humble oneself under the mighty hand of God. Anxiety is often a form of pride: an insistence on holding what one cannot control.

Luke 10:41 keeps the whole subject kind. Martha is not rebuked for working, and the meal she was making was for the Lord Himself; the trouble is that she was careful and troubled about many things, and the remedy offered is not idleness but proportion — one thing is needful. The Lord says her name twice, which is what He does when something matters and the person is loved. Whoever brings this doctrine to an anxious believer should notice that tone and copy it, because the passage is a correction delivered inside a friendship.
roots_summary: Greek merimnao (G3309), to be anxious, take thought; merimna (G3308), care, anxiety; turbazo (G5182), to be troubled; epiripto (G1977), to cast upon.
roots_lines: Greek merimnao (G3309) — to be anxious; Philippians 4:6, Matthew 6:25–34, Luke 10:41, 1 Corinthians 7:32.
Greek epiripsantes (G1977) — having cast upon; 1 Peter 5:7, Luke 19:35.
Greek melei auto peri humon (G3199) — it matters to him concerning you; 1 Peter 5:7.
usage: “Be careful for nothing; but in every thing by prayer” — the care is moved, not extinguished.
“For he careth for you” — two different words, and that is the argument.
“Martha, Martha” — the name twice, inside a friendship.

pos: n. (uneasiness under delay or suffering; the refusal to wait for God's time)
etymology: Latin impatientia, from in-, not, and pati, to suffer — an unwillingness to undergo. The biblical opposite is longsuffering, which keeps the root visible in English.
biblical_def: Impatience is the refusal to wait. James sets the farmer against it: “Be patient therefore, brethren, unto the coming of the Lord. Behold, the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it” (Jas 5:7). Saul's ruin is dated to an act of it: “I forced myself therefore, and offered a burnt offering” (1Sa 13:12), and Samuel's verdict follows immediately. Sarai's is the domestic version: “the LORD hath restrained me from bearing: I pray thee, go in unto my maid” (Gen 16:2). The promises come by the other road: “followers of them who through faith and patience inherit the promises” (Heb 6:12). And the psalm gives the discipline: “Rest in the LORD, and wait patiently for him” (Psa 37:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines impatience as uneasiness under pain or suffering; the not enduring of pain with composure; restlessness occasioned by suffering positive evil, or by the absence of expected good.
webster_full: IMPATIENCE, n. Uneasiness under pain or suffering; the not enduring of pain with composure; restlessness occasioned by suffering positive evils, or the absence of expected good.
Impatience under sufferings is a species of rebellion against the government of God.
IMPATIENT, a. Uneasy or fretful under suffering; not bearing pain with composure.
scriptures: Jas 5:7

Be patient therefore, brethren, unto the coming of the Lord. Behold, the husbandman waiteth for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it, until he receive the early and latter rain.
Therefore said I, The Philistines will come down now upon me to Gilgal, and I have not made supplication unto the LORD: I forced myself therefore, and offered a burnt offering.
Gen 16:2

And Sarai said unto Abram, Behold now, the LORD hath restrained me from bearing: I pray thee, go in unto my maid; it may be that I may obtain children by her. And Abram hearkened to the voice of Sarai.
Heb 6:12
That ye be not slothful, but followers of them who through faith and patience inherit the promises.
Psa 37:7
Rest in the LORD, and wait patiently for him: fret not thyself because of him who prospereth in his way, because of the man who bringeth wicked devices to pass.
corruption_summary: Impatience presents itself as initiative, and both of Scripture's great examples of it produced something that lasted for centuries.
corruption_paragraphs: Saul and Sarai are the two set pieces and they share a structure. In each, the situation is genuinely urgent — an army scattering, a womb that has not opened for decades. In each, the delay has run past what any reasonable person could be asked to bear. In each, the person acts, and the action is not obviously wicked: Saul offers a sacrifice, Sarai provides her husband an heir by the customary legal means of her culture. And in each, the consequence outlives them. Saul loses a kingdom; Sarai's expedient is still generating conflict. Impatience rarely looks like sin at the moment of decision. It looks like taking responsibility.

Webster's second line is worth the whole entry and is unusually theological for a dictionary: impatience under sufferings is a species of rebellion against the government of God. That names what is underneath. To be impatient is to have concluded that the timing is wrong, and the timing belongs to Someone. This is why Psalm 37:7 puts rest and waiting in the same breath — rest in the LORD, and wait patiently for him — and why the verses around it forbid fretting because of the man who prospers in his way. The waiting is bearable only on the assumption that the delay is governed.

James 5:7 supplies the picture that makes patience intelligible rather than merely commanded. The husbandman waits for the precious fruit of the earth, and hath long patience for it, until he receive the early and latter rain. He is not passive — he has ploughed, sown and will reap — and he is entirely unable to make anything grow faster. That is the Christian's position in nearly every important thing: real work to do, no control of the timetable, and a harvest promised. Hebrews 6:12 says the promises are inherited through faith and patience, which are named together because in practice they are the same act performed over time.
roots_summary: Greek makrothumia (G3115), longsuffering, long-temperedness; hupomone (G5281), endurance, patience; Hebrew aphaq (H662), to force oneself; chul (H2342), to wait, be in anguish.
roots_lines: Greek makrothumeo (G3114) — to be longsuffering, patient; James 5:7–8, 1 Thessalonians 5:14, 2 Peter 3:9.
Greek hupomone (G5281) — endurance under load; Hebrews 6:12, 10:36, Romans 5:3–4, James 1:3–4.
Hebrew ethappaq (H662) — I forced myself; 1 Samuel 13:12, Genesis 43:31, Isaiah 42:14.
usage: “I forced myself therefore” — and the kingdom went with it.
“The husbandman waiteth… and hath long patience” — working, and unable to hurry it.
“Rest in the LORD, and wait patiently” — rest and waiting, in one breath.

pos: v. (to rest satisfied in; to submit quietly to what one cannot or ought not to alter)
etymology: Latin acquiescere, to come to rest, from ad- and quies, rest. The word carries rest rather than defeat — a mind that has stopped struggling because it has found something to lean on.
biblical_def: To acquiesce is to come to rest in God's will. Job does it at the point of total loss: “the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD” (Job 1:21). Eli does it under a sentence on his house: “It is the LORD: let him do what seemeth him good” (1Sa 3:18). David does it fleeing his own son: “behold, here am I, let him do to me as seemeth good unto him” (2Sa 15:26). Paul says it is learned: “I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content” (Php 4:11). And the Lord does it in Gethsemane, having first asked for the cup to pass: “nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt” (Mat 26:39).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines acquiesce as to rest satisfied, or apparently satisfied, or to rest without opposition and discontent; to assent or submit.
webster_full: ACQUIESCE, v.i. To rest satisfied, or apparently satisfied, or to rest without opposition and discontent; usually implying previous opposition, uneasiness, or dislike, but ultimately a rest or satisfaction of mind.
ACQUIESCENCE, n. A quiet assent; a silent submission, or submission with apparent content.
scriptures: Job 1:21
And said, Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return thither: the LORD gave, and the LORD hath taken away; blessed be the name of the LORD.
And Samuel told him every whit, and hid nothing from him. And he said, It is the LORD: let him do what seemeth him good.
But if he thus say, I have no delight in thee; behold, here am I, let him do to me as seemeth good unto him.
Php 4:11
Not that I speak in respect of want: for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.
And he went a little further, and fell on his face, and prayed, saying, O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt.
corruption_summary: Acquiescence is confused with fatalism, and Gethsemane shows a request made in full before the submission is made at all.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster's definition contains the crucial phrase: usually implying previous opposition, uneasiness, or dislike, but ultimately a rest or satisfaction of mind. There is a struggle in the word. Christian acquiescence is not the flat compliance of a man with no preference; it is what a man arrives at, and Gethsemane is the pattern. The Lord asks — three times — that the cup pass from Him, with sweat as it were great drops of blood. Only then, nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt. The asking is not a failure of submission; it is where submission begins, and any doctrine of resignation that forbids the asking has not read the account.

Job 1:21 is often quoted as though it came easily, and the book exists to show that it did not. He says it having torn his mantle and shaved his head — the full formal expression of grief — and he says it before the argument of the next forty chapters, in which he protests, complains and demands a hearing without ever being rebuked for those. God's eventual reproof is not for the complaining but for the darkening of counsel by words without knowledge, and God's verdict on Job's speech at the end is that he spoke of Him the thing that was right.

The false version is fatalism, which arrives at the same words by a different road: nothing can be changed, so nothing should be asked. Scripture forbids that by commanding prayer, by recording Hezekiah's fifteen added years and the widow who wearied the unjust judge, and by the Lord's own request in the garden. The believer prays as though the outcome depended on it and rests as though it did not, and the two are held together by trusting the Person who decides. Philippians 4:11 calls the resulting state something Paul learned — which means it was not native to him, and that there is a curriculum.
roots_summary: Greek autarkes (G842), self-sufficient, content; plen (G4133), nevertheless; Hebrew tob be'enav (H2896), good in his eyes; barak (H1288), to bless.
roots_lines: Greek autarkes (G842) — content, sufficient; Philippians 4:11 only; the noun autarkeia, 1 Timothy 6:6, 2 Corinthians 9:8.
Greek plen ouch hos ego thelo (G4133) — nevertheless, not as I will; Matthew 26:39, Luke 22:42.
Hebrew ya'aseh hattob be'enav (H2896) — let him do what seemeth good in his eyes; 1 Samuel 3:18, 2 Samuel 15:26, 10:12.
usage: “Blessed be the name of the LORD” — said with a torn mantle.
“Nevertheless not as I will” — and He had asked first, three times.
“I have learned… to be content” — learned, so there is a curriculum.

pos: n. (approbation loudly expressed; the praise of men as an object of desire)
etymology: Latin applaudere, to clap the hands at. Scripture never forbids being well thought of; it forbids arranging one's life to secure it.
biblical_def: Applause is the praise of men. John names it as the reason rulers who believed would not confess Christ: “for they loved the praise of men more than the praise of God” (John 12:43). The Lord makes universal approval a warning sign: “Woe unto you, when all men shall speak well of you! for so did their fathers to the false prophets” (Luk 6:26). Paul makes it disqualifying for a servant: “for do I now persuade men, or God? or do I seek to please men? for if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ” (Gal 1:10); “not as pleasing men, but God, which trieth our hearts” (1Th 2:4). And Herod, receiving the shout, “gave not God the glory” (Act 12:22–23).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines applause as a shout of approbation; approbation and praise, publicly expressed by clapping the hands, acclamation or huzzas.
webster_full: APPLAUSE, n. A shout of approbation; approbation and praise, publicly expressed by clapping of hands, acclamation, huzzas, or other significant sign.
2. Approbation and commendation; praise.
APPLAUD, v.t. To praise by clapping the hands, acclamation, or other significant sign.
scriptures: John 12:43
For they loved the praise of men more than the praise of God.
Luk 6:26
Woe unto you, when all men shall speak well of you! for so did their fathers to the false prophets.
Gal 1:10
For do I now persuade men, or God? or do I seek to please men? for if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ.
But as we were allowed of God to be put in trust with the gospel, even so we speak; not as pleasing men, but God, which trieth our hearts.
And the people gave a shout, saying, It is the voice of a god, and not of a man.
corruption_summary: Popularity is read as evidence of God's blessing, and the Lord attached a woe to universal approval.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke 6:26 belongs to the same series as the beatitudes and is usually left out of the reading. Woe unto you, when all men shall speak well of you — and the reason given is historical rather than moral: for so did their fathers to the false prophets. Israel's popular preachers were the ones who said peace when there was no peace, and their popularity was earned honestly by telling people what they wanted. The verse does not say a well-liked man is a false teacher. It says that universal approval is the documented profile of one, and should be examined rather than enjoyed.

John 12:43 records the most tragic sentence in the Gospel and its subject is not the hostile. Among the chief rulers many believed on him, but because of the Pharisees they did not confess Him, lest they should be put out of the synagogue — for they loved the praise of men more than the praise of God. These were persuaded men. What stopped them was not the argument but the cost of the crowd's opinion, and the verse is placed at the end of the public ministry as its summary judgment. A great deal of unconfessed faith has died there since.

Galatians 1:10 shows what the question does to a ministry, and the tense matters: if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ. Paul is describing something he has left behind rather than a temptation he is currently resisting well, and the two loyalties are presented as exclusive. This is not an argument for being needlessly abrasive, which is its own vanity in reverse. It is a statement that the two audiences will eventually ask for different things, and a man cannot decide in the moment which he serves — he will do what he settled beforehand.
roots_summary: Greek doxa anthropon (G1391), the glory of men; areskein (G700), to please; anthropareskos (G441), a menpleaser; epiphoneo (G2019), to shout at, acclaim.
roots_lines: Greek doxan anthropon (G1391) — the praise, glory of men; John 12:43, 5:44, 1 Thessalonians 2:6.
Greek anthropareskos (G441) — menpleaser; Ephesians 6:6, Colossians 3:22.
Greek epephonei (G2019) — shouted, acclaimed; Acts 12:22, 21:34, 22:24.
usage: “When all men shall speak well of you” — the documented profile of a false prophet.
“They loved the praise of men more than the praise of God” — and they believed.
“If I yet pleased men” — and the two audiences will differ eventually.

pos: n. (expenditure beyond what a man has or ought; waste of substance)
etymology: Latin extra, beyond, and vagari, to wander — spending that has wandered outside its bounds. The prodigal's word in the AV is riotous living.
biblical_def: Extravagance is spending outside bounds. The prodigal “took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance with riotous living” (Luk 15:13); the unjust steward likewise “had wasted his goods” (Luk 16:1). Proverbs contrasts the two habits: “There is treasure to be desired and oil in the dwelling of the wise; but a foolish man spendeth it up” (Pro 21:20), and names the destination: “for the drunkard and the glutton shall come to poverty: and drowsiness shall clothe a man with rags” (Pro 23:21). Paul sets the floor of contentment low: “having food and raiment let us be therewith content” (1Ti 6:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines extravagance as excess of expenditure; the expending of money without necessity, or beyond one's means; prodigality; and, generally, any excess or exceeding of due bounds.
webster_full: EXTRAVAGANCE, n. A literal wandering beyond a limit; but in this sense not used.
2. Any excess or exceeding of due bounds; irregularity; wildness; as the extravagance of imagination.
3. Excess of expenditure; the expending of money without necessity, or beyond what is reasonable or proper; prodigality; as extravagance of the table.
scriptures: And not many days after the younger son gathered all together, and took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance with riotous living.
Luk 16:1
And he said also unto his disciples, There was a certain rich man, which had a steward; and the same was accused unto him that he had wasted his goods.
There is treasure to be desired and oil in the dwelling of the wise; but a foolish man spendeth it up.
For the drunkard and the glutton shall come to poverty: and drowsiness shall clothe a man with rags.
And having food and raiment let us be therewith content.
corruption_summary: The charge is aimed at other people's spending, and the parable makes the elder brother's accounting its second problem.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke 15 is the great treatment and the Lord does not stop where a sermon on thrift would. The younger son wastes his substance with riotous living, comes to want, and returns; and the father's response is a robe, a ring, shoes and the fatted calf — which is itself an extravagance, deliberately so, in a story about the cost of extravagance. Then the elder brother arrives with an exact ledger: these many years do I serve thee, neither transgressed I at any time thy commandment, and thou never gavest me a kid. The parable ends with him outside, and the father pleading. Careful accounting is not the moral of the story.

That said, the parable does not soften what the younger son did. He wasted what a lifetime of another man's labour had built, and he ended feeding swine and envying them, and the text says no man gave unto him. Extravagance is destructive precisely because it is pleasant, quick and answerable to no one until the money is gone; and Proverbs 21:20 puts the contrast in a domestic image — treasure and oil in the dwelling of the wise, and a foolish man who spendeth it up, which is exactly how it feels from inside, a steady consumption without a decision anywhere in it.

First Timothy 6:8 sets the floor lower than almost any Christian in a wealthy country lives, and it is worth letting it stand unqualified: having food and raiment, let us be therewith content. That is not a command to own nothing; the same letter tells the rich to do good, be rich in good works, ready to distribute, and says God giveth us richly all things to enjoy. It is a statement about where contentment is permitted to begin. A man whose contentment begins several tiers above food and raiment has not found the biblical floor, and everything above it will be experienced as necessity rather than gift.
roots_summary: Greek asotos (G811), riotously, without saving; diaskorpizo (G1287), to scatter, waste; arkeo (G714), to be sufficient; Hebrew bala (H1104), to swallow up.
roots_lines: Greek zon asotos (G811) — living riotously, wastefully; Luke 15:13 only; the noun asotia, Ephesians 5:18, Titus 1:6, 1 Peter 4:4.
Greek diaskorpizo (G1287) — to scatter, squander; Luke 15:13, 16:1, Matthew 25:24.
Greek arkesthesometha (G714) — we shall be content, it suffices; 1 Timothy 6:8, Hebrews 13:5.
usage: “Wasted his substance with riotous living” — and no man gave unto him.
“A foolish man spendeth it up” — a consumption with no decision in it.
“Having food and raiment” — where contentment is permitted to begin.

pos: n. (treachery; the breach of faith by one who was trusted)
etymology: Latin perfidia, from per-, through or amiss, and fides, faith — faith gone wrong. Perfidy is distinguished from mere enmity by the relationship it violates: only a friend can commit it.
biblical_def: Perfidy is betrayal by the trusted. God uses it of Israel: “Surely as a wife treacherously departeth from her husband, so have ye dealt treacherously with me, O house of Israel” (Jer 3:20). Malachi uses it of husbands: “yet is she thy companion, and the wife of thy covenant… therefore take heed to your spirit, and let none deal treacherously” (Mal 2:14–15). The psalm gives the grief exactly: “it was not an enemy that reproached me… but it was thou, a man mine equal, my guide, and mine acquaintance. We took sweet counsel together, and walked unto the house of God in company” (Psa 55:12–14). Proverbs weighs it: “Confidence in an unfaithful man in time of trouble is like a broken tooth, and a foot out of joint” (Pro 25:19). And Judas gave a kiss (Mat 26:49).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines perfidy as the act of violating faith, a promise, vow or allegiance; treachery; the violation of a trust reposed.
webster_full: PERFIDY, n. The act of violating faith, a promise, vow or allegiance; treachery; the violation of a trust reposed.
The word is applied to violations of a trust or confidence reposed by a friend, or to the breach of national faith.
PERFIDIOUS, a. Violating good faith or vows; false to trust or confidence reposed; treacherous.
scriptures: Jer 3:20
Surely as a wife treacherously departeth from her husband, so have ye dealt treacherously with me, O house of Israel, saith the LORD.
Mal 2:14
Yet ye say, Wherefore? Because the LORD hath been witness between thee and the wife of thy youth, against whom thou hast dealt treacherously: yet is she thy companion, and the wife of thy covenant.
For it was not an enemy that reproached me; then I could have borne it: neither was it he that hated me that did magnify himself against me; then I would have hid myself from him:
Confidence in an unfaithful man in time of trouble is like a broken tooth, and a foot out of joint.
And forthwith he came to Jesus, and said, Hail, master; and kissed him.
corruption_summary: Betrayal is treated as a private injury, and Scripture puts it in covenant language because a covenant is what was broken.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 55 is the passage to give someone who has been betrayed by a friend, because it refuses to minimise anything. If it had been an enemy, David says, then I could have borne it — the difference is not the damage but the source. It was thou, a man mine equal, my guide, mine acquaintance; we took sweet counsel together and walked unto the house of God in company. The last clause is the wound: they had worshipped together. Scripture does not tell the betrayed to reclassify this as an ordinary disappointment; it gives him a psalm in which the particular horror of it is spoken aloud to God.

Malachi 2 shows why the Bible reaches for covenant language rather than the language of hurt feelings. The men of Judah had dealt treacherously with the wives of their youth, and God's argument is that a covenant is a third party's business: the LORD hath been witness between thee and the wife of thy covenant. That is what makes perfidy more than a private matter. Vows are made before God, and He is in the room when they are broken, which is why the chapter says He no longer regards the offerings of men who do this.

Judas is the terminal case and the Gospels record it in a way that keeps the friendship in view. He is one of the twelve, a phrase repeated at every stage; he had the bag, sat at the supper, took the sop from the Lord's own hand. And the sign he chose was a kiss, to which the Lord replies, Friend, wherefore art thou come? The consolation for anyone betrayed is not that it did not matter but that the Lord has been there, in the sharpest form the experience takes, and knows it from the inside.
roots_summary: Hebrew bagad (H898), to deal treacherously; berith (H1285), covenant; Greek paradidomi (G3860), to deliver up, betray; kataphileo (G2705), to kiss fervently.
roots_lines: Hebrew bagad (H898) — to deal treacherously; Jeremiah 3:20, Malachi 2:14–16, Proverbs 25:19, Psalm 78:57.
Greek paradidomi (G3860) — to hand over, betray; Matthew 26:15–48, John 13:2, 1 Corinthians 11:23.
Greek kataphileo (G2705) — to kiss earnestly; Matthew 26:49, Luke 7:38, 15:20 — the father's kiss, and Judas's.
usage: “Then I could have borne it” — if it had been an enemy.
“The LORD hath been witness between thee and the wife of thy covenant”.
“Friend, wherefore art thou come?” — said to the man with the kiss.

pos: adj. (grand in appearance or scale; splendid — the AV's forms are magnifical and magnificence)
etymology: Latin magnus, great, and facere, to make — making great. The AV has magnifical of the temple David planned (1Ch 22:5) and magnificence of the temple of Diana (Act 19:27).
biblical_def: Magnificent is greatness made visible. David gives the reason for building on a scale: “the house that is to be builded for the LORD must be exceeding magnifical, of fame and of glory throughout all countries” (1Ch 22:5). The word's other appearance is a warning: Demetrius fears that the temple of Diana “should be despised, and her magnificence should be destroyed” (Act 19:27) — the same splendour, spent on an idol. The psalm supplies the proper object: “I will speak of the glorious honour of thy majesty, and of thy wondrous works” (Psa 145:5). And Solomon, dedicating the finished house, says what no builder can escape: “the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain thee; how much less this house that I have builded?” (1Ki 8:27).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines magnificent as grand in appearance; splendid; pompous; exhibiting greatness; and, of God, exalted in dignity, august in works.
webster_full: MAGNIFICENT, a. Grand in appearance; splendid; pompous; exhibiting greatness, particularly in buildings, equipage, retinue, or the like.
2. Exhibiting grandeur of thought or sentiment; sublime.
MAGNIFICENCE, n. Grandeur of appearance; greatness and splendor of show or state.
scriptures: And David said, Solomon my son is young and tender, and the house that is to be builded for the LORD must be exceeding magnifical, of fame and of glory throughout all countries: I will therefore now make preparation for it. So David prepared abundantly before his death.

So that not only this our craft is in danger to be set at nought; but also that the temple of the great goddess Diana should be despised, and her magnificence should be destroyed, whom all Asia and the world worshippeth.
I will speak of the glorious honour of thy majesty, and of thy wondrous works.
But will God indeed dwell on the earth? behold, the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain thee; how much less this house that I have builded?
Mar 13:1
And as he went out of the temple, one of his disciples saith unto him, Master, see what manner of stones and what buildings are here!
corruption_summary: Splendour in worship is treated as always right or always wrong, and Scripture commands one temple and lets another be thrown down.
corruption_paragraphs: The Bible will not support either party in the argument over beauty in worship. God specified the tabernacle's gold, blue, purple and scarlet down to the pomegranates on the hem, filled a craftsman with His Spirit for the work, and approved David's intention that the house be exceeding magnifical. He also let that house be destroyed twice, told a woman at a well that the hour was coming when neither in this mountain nor at Jerusalem would men worship the Father, and answered a disciple admiring the stonework with a prediction that not one stone would be left upon another.

First Kings 8:27 is the sentence that keeps magnificence honest, and it is spoken by the man who built the thing, at the moment of its dedication, with the glory filling the house: the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain thee; how much less this house that I have builded? Solomon is not disparaging his own work. He is saying what every builder must know — that the building is a gesture, not a container, and the moment a congregation mistakes the two the splendour has begun to function as an idol rather than a signpost.

Acts 19:27 supplies the negative image and it is unsettling how similar it is. Demetrius's concern for the magnificence of Diana's temple is genuine civic piety and it was also a livelihood, and the two were impossible to separate even for him. That is the standing danger of religious splendour: it accumulates constituencies. Anyone deciding what a church spends should be able to say who benefits and what the beauty is pointing at, and Psalm 145:5 gives the only answer that justifies the expense — that men should speak of the glorious honour of thy majesty.
roots_summary: Hebrew gadal lemaalah (H1431), exceeding great, magnifical; hod (H1935), majesty, honour; Greek megaleiotes (G3168), magnificence, majesty; doxa (G1391), glory.
roots_lines: Hebrew lehagdil lemaalah (H1431) — to make exceeding great, magnifical; 1 Chronicles 22:5, 29:25.
Greek megaleiotes (G3168) — magnificence, majesty; Acts 19:27, Luke 9:43, 2 Peter 1:16.
Hebrew hadar kebod hodeka (H1926, H3519, H1935) — the glorious honour of thy majesty; Psalm 145:5.
usage: “Must be exceeding magnifical” — and God approved the intention.
“Her magnificence should be destroyed” — the same splendour, spent on Diana.
“How much less this house that I have builded?” — said by the builder, at the dedication.

pos: n. (the land of the Hellenes; in prophecy, the third of Daniel's four kingdoms; the AV also has Grecia)
etymology: Latin Graecia. The AV uses Grecia in Daniel and Zechariah and Greece in Acts, and calls its people Greeks or Grecians — the latter often for Greek-speaking Jews.
biblical_def: Greece is the Hellenic world. Paul travelled there: “when he had gone over those parts, and had given them much exhortation, he came into Greece” (Act 20:2), and at Athens “his spirit was stirred in him, when he saw the city wholly given to idolatry” (Act 17:16). Daniel names it in prophecy before its rise: “the rough goat is the king of Grecia” (Dan 8:21). Zechariah sets Zion against it: “and raised up thy sons, O Zion, against thy sons, O Greece” (Zec 9:13). And Greeks come looking for Christ at the last Passover: “Sir, we would see Jesus” (John 12:20–21).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Grecian as pertaining to Greece; and Greek as a native of Greece, or the language of Greece, which is one of the most perfect of languages.
webster_full: GRECIAN, a. Pertaining to Greece.
GRECIAN, n. A native of Greece; also, a Jew who understood Greek; and a scholar versed in the Greek language.
GREEK, n. A native of Greece.
2. The language of Greece.
scriptures: Act 20:2
And when he had gone over those parts, and had given them much exhortation, he came into Greece,
Now while Paul waited for them at Athens, his spirit was stirred in him, when he saw the city wholly given to idolatry.
Dan 8:21
And the rough goat is the king of Grecia: and the great horn that is between his eyes is the first king.
Zec 9:13
When I have bent Judah for me, filled the bow with Ephraim, and raised up thy sons, O Zion, against thy sons, O Greece, and made thee as the sword of a mighty man.
John 12:20
And there were certain Greeks among them that came up to worship at the feast:
corruption_summary: Greece is treated as the church's cultural enemy or as its philosophical foundation, and the New Testament used its language while refusing its wisdom.
corruption_paragraphs: The providence is worth stating plainly because it cuts against both simple positions. Alexander's conquests gave the Mediterranean world a common tongue; three centuries later the apostles wrote the New Testament in it, and the Old Testament had already been translated into it at Alexandria. The gospel travelled on Greek roads, in Greek, to cities Greek colonists had built. A Christian who despises Greece has to explain why the Spirit chose its language, and why Paul quoted its poets on Mars' hill.

The other reading goes too far the other way, treating Athens as a preparation the gospel merely completed. First Corinthians 1 forecloses that: the Greeks seek after wisdom, and Christ crucified is unto the Greeks foolishness. Paul is not saying they lacked information; he is saying the cross does not fit inside the category of wisdom they had built, and cannot be made to. Acts 17 ends with the sermon breaking on exactly that point — when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked.

Acts 17:16 gives the personal note that keeps the subject from being an abstraction. Paul walks into the most beautiful city in the ancient world, and his spirit is stirred in him — provoked, exasperated — because he saw it wholly given to idolatry. He did not see the architecture first. Then in John 12 the movement runs the other way: Greeks come up to the feast and ask Philip, Sir, we would see Jesus — and the Lord answers that the hour is come that the Son of man should be glorified, and speaks of a corn of wheat falling into the ground and dying. The Greeks got their answer, and it was the cross.
roots_summary: Greek Hellas (G1671), Greece; Hellen (G1672), a Greek; Hellenistes (G1675), a Grecian, Greek-speaking Jew; Hebrew Yavan (H3120), Javan, Greece.

Hebrew Yavan (H3120) — Javan, Greece; Daniel 8:21, 10:20, Zechariah 9:13, Genesis 10:2.

“His spirit was stirred in him” — he did not see the architecture first.
“Sir, we would see Jesus” — and the answer was a corn of wheat, and the cross.
